Day-of-week / value-day pricing tiers never mentioned on a Tuesday move

top_strength: This is the best insurance explanation in either of Bri's calls this week, and she earned it by listening. The customer opened with an unprompted story about a previous mover shattering an 85-inch TV and offering $100, and Bri answered the actual grievance rather than reciting the benefit: "Texas only has a state mandated 60¢ per pound coverage just so you know, our no worries. Damage coverage is free included in our hourly rate, and it provides up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace or reimburse for accidental damages." She then went further than the rubric asks and offered the concrete fix — the TV bag that "holds up to a sixty inch TV" with its own space on the truck. The On-Time Guarantee is also fully delivered here, not just named: "if we can't make it in the time window that we arrange, we immediately start discounting money of your final bill." And she closed the wrap-quality anxiety properly, telling the customer how to make the protection stick on move day: "please feel free to use your voice when you get there to reiterate that I have noted it. The movers always read the notes before and they call and confirm the day before."
coaching_note: The customer booked this move without ever being told the hourly rate. Bri gave a dollar range and a trip fee, and only explained what an hourly rate covers 15 minutes later when the customer asked about blanket charges — "we actually just charge an hourly rate. Everything's included in the hourly rate" — still without a number. That is the single highest-value fix: state the rate, the crew, and what's included before the estimate range, not after, or the range reads as a made-up number and every included item sounds like it might not be. Second, the entire Save Your Ass speech is missing on the one call this week where it would have paid most — this is a three-stop move with four bed sets to break down, carry upstairs and reassemble, and there was never a word about prep shortening the billed clock. That likely also explains why the 4.5–5.5 hour estimate looks light: stairs, the elevator at storage and the assembly time never entered the math out loud. Across both of Bri's calls the same four bullets fall out every time — no "how are you," no "sound good," almost no name use, and no hours given — which is habit, not tenure. She is three months in and the hard mechanics are already solid; what she needs is a pre-call checklist for the last line of each script, not more reps.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and genuinely responsive — she met the damaged-TV story with "So I am so sorry that you did that" and a solution rather than moving on, defused a painfully long gate-code exchange with "wow they're really testing us there," and closed on real interest in the customer's plan ("All good for you. Excited for your change"); short of a 5 only because the name goes unused until the sign-off and the bed-inventory section turned mechanical enough that she had to correct herself twice.
